results.authors: Stupp R, Mason WP, van den Bent MJ, et al.
results.key_finding: The Stupp protocol established the standard of care: maximal safe surgical resection followed by concurrent radiotherapy (60 Gy in 30 fractions) with daily temozolomide (75 mg/m2), then 6 cycles of adjuvant temozolomide (150-200 mg/m2, days 1-5 of each 28-day cycle). Median overall survival improved from 12.1 to 14.6 months.
results.title: Radiotherapy plus Concomitant and Adjuvant Temozolomide for Glioblastoma

results.authors: Stupp R, Taillibert S, Kanner A, et al.
results.key_finding: Addition of tumor-treating fields (TTFields) to maintenance temozolomide improved median overall survival to 20.9 months vs 16.0 months. TTFields is now considered part of the standard of care for newly diagnosed GBM.
results.title: Effect of Tumor-Treating Fields Plus Maintenance Temozolomide vs Maintenance Temozolomide Alone on Survival in Patients With Glioblastoma: A Randomized Clinical Trial (EF-14)

results.key_finding: Standard of care for newly diagnosed GBM: maximal safe resection, followed by RT (60 Gy) + concurrent TMZ, then adjuvant TMZ + TTFields. For MGMT unmethylated tumors, temozolomide benefit is reduced but still recommended. Clinical trial enrollment should be offered.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Tiffany Coleman is a 64-year-old right-handed woman and high school math teacher who presents to the emergency department after experiencing a witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure at home approximately 2 hours ago. Her wife reports that the seizure lasted roughly 90 seconds and was preceded by her left arm stiffening and shaking for about 15 seconds before becoming generalized. She was post-ictal and confused for approximately 20 minutes before regaining conversational ability, although her wife notes she has still not returned to her baseline. There was no tongue bite or urinary incontinence. She has no prior history of seizures. On further questioning, her wife describes a 3-week history of progressively worsening headaches, initially attributed by their primary care physician to tension-type headaches and treated with ibuprofen. These headaches are worst in the morning upon waking, are dull and pressure-like, and have been accompanied by nausea on several occasions, with two episodes of vomiting over the past week. She also reports that over the past 2 weeks, she has developed noticeable weakness of her left arm, initially manifesting as difficulty buttoning her shirt and clumsiness when writing on the blackboard with her left hand for emphasis. Her colleagues at school remarked that she seemed to be struggling to find the right words during her lectures, something entirely out of character for a woman known for her articulate teaching style. Over the past week, her wife has noticed she seems more forgetful and occasionally confused, once becoming disoriented briefly while driving on a familiar route home from school. She was placed on medical leave from teaching five days ago after an episode where she lost her train of thought mid-sentence during a parent-teacher conference. She denies recent fever, chills, night sweats, or significant weight loss, although her wife thinks she may have lost a few pounds over the past month due to decreased appetite from the nausea.
